claim: The hippocampal–entorhinal system encodes a map of space that guides spatial navigation.
source: The hippocampal–entorhinal system encodes a map of space that guides spatial navigation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established background knowledge about the hippocampal-entorhinal system.

claim: Goal-directed behaviour outside of spatial navigation requires a representation of abstract forms of relational knowledge.
source: Goal-directed behaviour outside of spatial navigation similarly requires a representation of abstract forms of relational knowledge.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract.

claim: Abstract relational knowledge relies on the same neural system as spatial navigation.
source: This information relies on the same neural system, but it is not known whether the organisational principles governing continuous maps may extend to the implicit encoding of discrete, non-spatial graphs.
evidence: The manuscript states this as background knowledge while noting the gap in understanding.

claim: The human hippocampal–entorhinal system can represent relationships between objects using a metric that depends on associative strength.
source: Here, we show that the human hippocampal–entorhinal system can represent relationships between objects using a metric that depends on associative strength.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by fMRI data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A map-like knowledge structure can be reconstructed directly from hippocampal–entorhinal fMRI adaptation signals.
source: We reconstruct a map-like knowledge structure directly from a hippocampal–entorhinal functional magnetic resonance imaging adaptation signal in a situation where relationships are non-spatial rather than spatial, discrete rather than continuous, and unavailable to conscious awareness.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through the MDS analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The measure that best predicted behavioral signature of implicit knowledge was a weighted sum of future states, akin to the successor representation.
source: Notably, the measure that best predicted a behavioural signature of implicit knowledge and blood oxygen level-dependent adaptation was a weighted sum of future states, akin to the successor representation that has been proposed to account for place and grid-cell firing patterns.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the behavioral data in Figure 5 and fMRI data in Figure 4.

claim: Spatially tuned cells in the hippocampal–entorhinal system have precise place codes.
source: In physical space, spatially tuned cells in the hippocampal–entorhinal system have precise place (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971) and grid (Hafting et al., 2005) codes that may form the neural basis of a 'cognitive map' (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This is cited background knowledge from O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971.

claim: Spatially tuned cells in the hippocampal–entorhinal system have precise grid codes.
source: In physical space, spatially tuned cells in the hippocampal–entorhinal system have precise place (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971) and grid (Hafting et al., 2005) codes that may form the neural basis of a 'cognitive map' (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This is cited background knowledge from Hafting et al., 2005.

claim: Place and grid codes may form the neural basis of a 'cognitive map'.
source: In physical space, spatially tuned cells in the hippocampal–entorhinal system have precise place (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971) and grid (Hafting et al., 2005) codes that may form the neural basis of a 'cognitive map' (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This is cited background knowledge from O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978.

claim: The particular form of place and grid representations enables rapid computations of spatial relationships such as distances and vector paths.
source: It is likely that the particular form of these representations enables rapid computations of spatial relationships such as distances and vector paths (Bush et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Bush et al., 2015 and Stemmler et al., 2015.

claim: Animals can find novel paths through space.
source: The potential for such rapid online computations embedded into neuronal representations may explain how animals can find novel paths through space (McNaughton et al., 2006; Mittelstaedt and Mittelstaedt, 1980) or rapidly reroute when obstacles are introduced (Alvernhe et al., 2011) or removed (Alvernhe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from McNaughton et al., 2006 and Mittelstaedt and Mittelstaedt, 1980.

claim: Animals can rapidly reroute when obstacles are introduced.
source: The potential for such rapid online computations embedded into neuronal representations may explain how animals can find novel paths through space (McNaughton et al., 2006; Mittelstaedt and Mittelstaedt, 1980) or rapidly reroute when obstacles are introduced (Alvernhe et al., 2011) or removed (Alvernhe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Alvernhe et al., 2011.

claim: Animals can rapidly reroute when obstacles are removed.
source: The potential for such rapid online computations embedded into neuronal representations may explain how animals can find novel paths through space (McNaughton et al., 2006; Mittelstaedt and Mittelstaedt, 1980) or rapidly reroute when obstacles are introduced (Alvernhe et al., 2011) or removed (Alvernhe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Alvernhe et al., 2008.

claim: In humans, signals that encode distance metrics between landmarks can be read out directly from fMRI data in the entorhinal cortex.
source: Indeed, in humans, signals that encode distance metrics between landmarks (Howard et al., 2014; Morgan et al., 2011) and directions to goals (Chadwick et al., 2015) can be read out directly from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data in the entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This is cited from Howard et al., 2014 and Morgan et al., 2011.

claim: In humans, signals that encode directions to goals can be read out directly from fMRI data in the entorhinal cortex.
source: Indeed, in humans, signals that encode distance metrics between landmarks (Howard et al., 2014; Morgan et al., 2011) and directions to goals (Chadwick et al., 2015) can be read out directly from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data in the entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This is cited from Chadwick et al., 2015.

claim: The hippocampal formation encodes non-spatial relationships between objects.
source: The hippocampal formation also encodes non-spatial relationships between objects.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge and supported by citations in the following sentences.

claim: When objects can be laid out in a continuous dimension such as time, hippocampal codes reflect proximity along this dimension.
source: When these objects can be laid out in a continuous dimension such as time, hippocampal codes extracted from neuronal ensembles (Rubin et al., 2015) or fMRI voxel patterns (Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014) reflect proximity along this dimension.
evidence: This is cited from Rubin et al., 2015 and Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014.

claim: fMRI signals reflect veridical angles when two-dimensional abstract spaces are formed from continuous dimensions.
source: fMRI signals also appear to reflect veridical angles when two-dimensional abstract spaces are formed from continuous dimensions (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Tavares et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Constantinescu et al., 2016 and Tavares et al., 2015.

claim: Many relationships encoded by the hippocampal formation reflect associations or relationships between discrete objects.
source: However, many relationships that are encoded by the hippocampal formation reflect associations or relationships between discrete objects (Horner et al., 2015; Schapiro et al., 2013, 2012; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Horner et al., 2015; Schapiro et al., 2013, 2012; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012.

claim: It is unclear how associative structures might be represented in the absence of a continuous organising dimension such as space or time.
source: To be a useful source of knowledge, many associations must be organised within an associative structure, but it is unclear how such structures might be represented in the absence of a continuous organising dimension such as space or time.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Highly complex relational structures are often learnt implicitly.
source: Highly complex relational structures are often learnt implicitly i.e. unintentionally and without explicit awareness (Cleeremans et al., 1998; Reber, 1989; Seger and Augart, 1994).
evidence: This is cited from Cleeremans et al., 1998; Reber, 1989; Seger and Augart, 1994.

claim: Implicitly acquired relational knowledge can be reflected as increases in neural similarity for pairwise associations in the temporal cortex.
source: Neurally, implicitly acquired relational knowledge can be reflected as increases in neural similarity for pairwise associations in the temporal cortex (Schapiro et al., 2012) or for members of a temporal community structure (Schapiro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Schapiro et al., 2012.

claim: Implicitly acquired relational knowledge can be reflected as increases in neural similarity for members of a temporal community structure.
source: Neurally, implicitly acquired relational knowledge can be reflected as increases in neural similarity for pairwise associations in the temporal cortex (Schapiro et al., 2012) or for members of a temporal community structure (Schapiro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Schapiro et al., 2013.

claim: It is unclear whether map- or graph-like knowledge structures might be encoded non-consciously.
source: However, it is unclear whether map- or graph-like knowledge structures might be encoded non-consciously, i.e. without subjects being aware of relationships between objects.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: 23 human participants were exposed to object sequences whose stimulus transitions were determined by a random walk in a graph.
source: We exposed 23 human participants to object sequences whose stimulus transitions, unbeknownst to them, were determined by a random walk in a graph (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Subjects performed a behavioral cover task in which they learned to associate a random stimulus orientation with a button press.
source: Subjects performed a behavioural cover task, in which they learned to associate a random stimulus orientation with a button press.
evidence: This describes the experimental task.

claim: After the fMRI experiment, subjects were debriefed and none reported any explicit knowledge of structure in the task.
source: After the fMRI experiment, subjects were debriefed and none reported any explicit knowledge of structure in the task.
evidence: This is reported as an observation from debriefing.

claim: Neither accuracy nor response time in the cover task depended on the object on screen or the transition structure.
source: Neither accuracy nor response time in this task depended on the object on screen or the transition structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: fMRI adaptation analysis revealed a cluster bilaterally in the entorhinal cortex where responses to each object increased as a linear function of the link distance of the preceding item.
source: This adaptation analysis revealed a cluster bilaterally in the entorhinal cortex (Figure 2A, family-wise error corrected at peak level within a bilateral entorhinal cortex/subiculum mask, left p=0.014, peak t22 = 4.42, [−18, –19, −22] and right p=0.006, peak t22 = 4.75, [24, −25, −22].
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The right entorhinal peak survived small volume correction for a larger ROI comprising the hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and entorhinal cortex.
source: A right, but not left peak also survived small volume correction (SVC) for a larger region of interest [ROI] comprising the hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and entorhinal cortex, left p=0.058 and right p=0.026, see ROIs in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis.

claim: The adaptation effect cannot be explained by basic statistics of the object sequence, such as the number of times an object occurred during training.
source: This adaptation effect cannot be explained by basic statistics of the object sequence, such as the number of times an object occurred during training, or basic features of the graph structure, such as the number of neighbours an object has on the graph (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by control analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The adaptation effect cannot be explained by basic features of the graph structure, such as the number of neighbours an object has on the graph.
source: This adaptation effect cannot be explained by basic statistics of the object sequence, such as the number of times an object occurred during training, or basic features of the graph structure, such as the number of neighbours an object has on the graph (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by control analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The fMRI adaptation faithfully represents the link distance.
source: This pair of tests suggests that the fMRI adaptation faithfully represents the link distance.
evidence: This is concluded from the orthogonal contrasts analysis shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Extracting data from an independent coordinate from Chadwick et al., 2015 revealed a linear effect of link distance.
source: Extracting data from this coordinate (ROI 3) revealed a linear effect of link distance (Figure 2E, F2,44 = 10.04, p<0.001), and correspondingly a significant difference between distances of lengths 1 and 3 (t22 = 3.71, p=0.001) and lengths 2 and 3 (t22 = 3.19, p=0.004), but not between distances of lengths 1 and 2 (t22 = 1.67, p=0.11).
evidence: This is a statistical result from an independent ROI analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: When temporal and distance relationships between pairs of objects were allowed to compete for variance, the number of links, but not time, explained the neural signal.
source: When the temporal and distance relationships between pairs of objects were allowed to compete for variance in a multiple linear regression, the number of links (t22 = 3.29, p=0.003), but not time (t22 = 1.27, p=0.22), explained the neural signal extracted from the independently defined ROI 3 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from a multiple regression analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The symmetrised distance measure, rather than the directional distance measure, predicted the fMRI suppression effect.
source: When allowing this measure to compete with its symmetrised, and thereby non-directional, self in a linear model, it was the symmetrised version alone that predicted the fMRI suppression effect (Figure 3C, t22 = 2.78, p=0.01 and t22 = −1.64, p=0.11).
evidence: This is a statistical result from a linear model analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When multidimensional scaling was applied to the fMRI distance matrix, the graph structure of the experimental map was recovered.
source: When we applied multidimensional scaling (MDS) in order to visualise the most faithful two-dimensional representation of distances in this matrix, the graph structure of our experimental map was recovered despite the subjects' professed ignorance of any such organisation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MDS analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The multidimensional scaling-mapped distances are significantly more correlated with link distances of the original graph structure than with link distances of a null distribution.
source: Permutation tests confirm that the multidimensional scaling-mapped distances are significantly more correlated with link distances of the original graph structure than with link distances of a null distribution consisting of all other complete graphs with seven links (r = 0.65, p=0.003, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from permutation tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No links cross in the graph resulting from the MDS mapping.
source: Furthermore, no links cross in the graph resulting from the MDS mapping.
evidence: This is an observation from the MDS analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Only 13.17% of all possible graphs with nodes in the same location but seven randomly distributed links are characterized by no line crossings.
source: This is only true for 13.17% of all possible graphs with nodes in the same location, but seven randomly distributed links (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from a permutation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The successor representation may facilitate reinforcement learning by enabling rapid computation of navigational trajectories.
source: The successor representation may facilitate reinforcement learning, because the resulting predictive measure of future states could be flexibly combined with reward representations to enable rapid computation of navigational trajectories (Baram et al., 2017; Dayan, 1993; Momennejad et al., 2016; Russek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Baram et al., 2017; Dayan, 1993; Momennejad et al., 2016; Russek et al., 2016.

claim: Neural activity bilaterally in the hippocampal–entorhinal system scales with communicability.
source: We find that neural activity bilaterally in the hippocampal–entorhinal system scales with communicability (Figure 4B, C, family-wise error corrected at peak level within a bilateral entorhinal cortex/subiculum mask, left p=0.001, peak t22 = 5.47 [−18, –19, −25] and right p=0.0005, peak t22 = 5.79, [21, −19, −28]).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Both hippocampal-entorhinal clusters showing communicability effects survived small volume correction for a larger ROI comprising the hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and entorhinal cortex.
source: Both clusters also survived SVC (small-volume correction) for a larger ROI comprising the hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and entorhinal cortex (left p=0.004 and right p=0.004, see ROIs in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis.

claim: In the left hippocampal formation, communicability effects are significant even if Euclidian distances are included as an additional regressor.
source: In the left hippocampal formation, communicability effects are significant even if Euclidian distances are included as an additional regressor (Figure 4D, p=0.006, peak t22 = 4.72, [−15, –13, −19], SVC mask 1 and p=0.027, SVC mask 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from a control analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The hippocampal–entorhinal system does not map the graph structure into a Euclidian space.
source: This suggests that the hippocampal–entorhinal system does not map the graph structure into a Euclidian space.
evidence: This is concluded from the analysis showing communicability effects remain significant when controlling for Euclidian distance.

claim: The distance effect observed in the hippocampal-entorhinal system may be a consequence of encoding a predictive representation of states within a graph structure.
source: Instead, these results are consistent with the view that the distance effect we observe in this system may be a consequence of the hippocampal formation encoding a predictive representation of states within a graph structure (Stachenfeld et al., 2016, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results citing Stachenfeld et al., 2016, 2014.

claim: An independent group of 26 participants was trained in the same way as the scanning cohort and asked to repeat the object orientation cover task on day 2.
source: To reveal such implicit learning behaviourally, we asked an independent group of 26 participants, who were trained in the same way as the scanning cohort on the first graph structure (Figure 5A), to repeat the object orientation cover task on day 2.
evidence: This describes the behavioral experiment design.

claim: Log-transformed response times were longer the further away the preceding object was on the graph.
source: Indeed, we found that log-transformed response times were longer the further away the preceding object was on the graph (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Response times scaled with communicability but not with link or Euclidian distance between objects.
source: In line with our imaging results, response times did not scale with link or Euclidian distance between objects, but instead with communicability (communicability: t25 = 2.77, p=0.01; link distance: t25 = −0.40, p=0.69; Euclidian distance: t25 = −0.85, p=0.40, Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral experiment shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The hippocampal–entorhinal system is engaged when an animal navigates within a physical environment and acquires flexible knowledge about spatial relationships.
source: The hippocampal–entorhinal system is engaged when an animal navigates within a physical environment and acquires flexible knowledge about spatial relationships.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Discussion.

claim: In mammals, the hippocampal–entorhinal system contributes to spatial navigation by mapping relationships in situations where knowledge is physical, continuous, and consciously available.
source: In mammals, the hippocampal–entorhinal system contributes to spatial navigation by mapping relationships in situations where knowledge is physical, continuous, and consciously available (Chadwick et al., 2015; Derdikman and Moser, 2010; Howard et al., 2014; Spiers and Maguire, 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Chadwick et al., 2015; Derdikman and Moser, 2010; Howard et al., 2014; Spiers and Maguire, 2007.

claim: The hippocampal–entorhinal system efficiently extracts statistical regularities in a non-spatial task where the relationships between items are discrete.
source: Here, we used a statistical learning paradigm to demonstrate that the hippocampal–entorhinal system also efficiently extracts statistical regularities in a non-spatial task where the relationships between items are discrete, and organises this non-spatial relational knowledge in an abstract relational map, suggesting that the hippocampal–entorhinal system creates metric representations of discrete relationships based on associative strengths (Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2014).
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The hippocampal–entorhinal system creates metric representations of discrete relationships based on associative strengths.
source: Here, we used a statistical learning paradigm to demonstrate that the hippocampal–entorhinal system also efficiently extracts statistical regularities in a non-spatial task where the relationships between items are discrete, and organises this non-spatial relational knowledge in an abstract relational map, suggesting that the hippocampal–entorhinal system creates metric representations of discrete relationships based on associative strengths (Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2014).
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the study's findings, citing Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2014.

claim: There were no continuous dimensions in the discrete stimulus sets used in the study.
source: Notably, there were no continuous dimensions in our discrete stimulus sets. The dimensions had to be extracted from the associations.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: The dimensions had to be extracted from the associations.
source: Notably, there were no continuous dimensions in our discrete stimulus sets. The dimensions had to be extracted from the associations.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design and what subjects had to do implicitly.

claim: The hippocampal formation maps experiences across a wide range of different dimensions, thereby supporting flexible behaviour across many domains of life.
source: These results add to the notion that the hippocampal formation maps experiences across a wide range of different dimensions, thereby supporting flexible behaviour across many domains of life (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Tolman, 1948).
evidence: This is cited from O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978 and Tolman, 1948.

claim: Recent studies have focused on the human hippocampal formation for storing the relational knowledge that makes up simple world models in reinforcement learning.
source: Recent studies have focused on the human hippocampal formation for storing the relational knowledge that makes up simple world models in reinforcement learning (Barron et al., 2013; Boorman et al., 2016; Bornstein and Daw, 2013; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Barron et al., 2013; Boorman et al., 2016; Bornstein and Daw, 2013; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012.

claim: The study's findings extend simple associative paradigms to more complex associative maps.
source: Our findings extend these simple associative paradigms to more complex associative maps, and demonstrate that these maps may be learnt implicitly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The maps may be learnt implicitly.
source: Our findings extend these simple associative paradigms to more complex associative maps, and demonstrate that these maps may be learnt implicitly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The resulting map is not Euclidian in nature.
source: Notably, the resulting map is not Euclidian in nature.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis showing communicability rather than Euclidian distance predicts the data.

claim: The neural data and behavior are consistent with a measure corresponding to a weighted sum of future states in the graph structure.
source: Instead, we find that the neural data as well as the behaviour are consistent with a measure corresponding to a weighted sum of future states in the graph structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analyses showing communicability and successor representation predict the data.

claim: Reinforcement learning benefits from knowledge about warped geometries in space, which may be represented as predictive maps, or successor representations, in the hippocampal formation.
source: This is consistent with the idea that reinforcement learning benefits from knowledge about warped geometries in space, which may be represented as predictive maps, or successor representations, in the hippocampal formation (Stachenfeld et al., 2016, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Stachenfeld et al., 2016, 2014.

claim: Predictive representations of the relationships between discrete objects or states of the world may be combined with reward representations to enable flexible goal-directed behaviour.
source: Such predictive representations of the relationships between discrete objects or states of the world may be combined with reward representations to enable flexible goal-directed behaviour (Baram et al., 2017; Dayan, 1993; Momennejad et al., 2016; Russek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Baram et al., 2017; Dayan, 1993; Momennejad et al., 2016; Russek et al., 2016.

claim: The map of the relational structure in discrete abstract space may be encoded by the pattern of firing in the entorhinal cortex.
source: Our data suggest that the map of the relational structure in discrete abstract space may be encoded by the pattern of firing in the entorhinal cortex, which also encodes maps in continuous physical space.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The entorhinal cortex is noted for the presence of grid cells.
source: The entorhinal cortex is noted for the presence of grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005), which may provide a metric for measuring distances in physical space (Bush et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015), allowing vector navigation.
evidence: This is cited from Hafting et al., 2005.

claim: Grid cells may provide a metric for measuring distances in physical space, allowing vector navigation.
source: The entorhinal cortex is noted for the presence of grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005), which may provide a metric for measuring distances in physical space (Bush et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015), allowing vector navigation.
evidence: This is cited from Bush et al., 2015 and Stemmler et al., 2015.

claim: Grid-like firing might be understood as a principal component decomposition of the covariance information between place cells.
source: However, recent theoretical treatments suggest that grid-like firing might also be understood as a principal component decomposition of the covariance information between place cells (Dordek et al., 2016) or the transitions between states (Stachenfeld et al., 2016, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Dordek et al., 2016.

claim: Grid-like firing might be understood as a principal component decomposition of the transitions between states.
source: However, recent theoretical treatments suggest that grid-like firing might also be understood as a principal component decomposition of the covariance information between place cells (Dordek et al., 2016) or the transitions between states (Stachenfeld et al., 2016, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Stachenfeld et al., 2016, 2014.

claim: Grid-like firing patterns could extend to discrete spaces.
source: Together with the finding of hippocampal cells in humans that encode individual concepts (which may be analogous to place cells), these theories can explain how grid-like firing patterns could extend to discrete spaces (such as the one we have used here), and also make predictions for how grid-like coding might extend to higher-dimensional spaces (Baram et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on theoretical work and the current findings, citing Baram et al., 2017.

claim: Grid-like coding might extend to higher-dimensional spaces.
source: Together with the finding of hippocampal cells in humans that encode individual concepts (which may be analogous to place cells), these theories can explain how grid-like firing patterns could extend to discrete spaces (such as the one we have used here), and also make predictions for how grid-like coding might extend to higher-dimensional spaces (Baram et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Baram et al., 2017.

claim: The human brain can acquire abstract knowledge unconsciously and automatically by extracting statistical regularities from incidental exposure to events generated according to a set of rules.
source: Our behavioural results are consistent with the observation that the human brain can acquire abstract knowledge unconsciously and automatically by extracting statistical regularities from incidental exposure to events generated according to a set of rules (Berry and Broadbent, 1984; Cleeremans et al., 1998; Reber, 1989, 1967; Seger and Augart, 1994).
evidence: This is cited from Berry and Broadbent, 1984; Cleeremans et al., 1998; Reber, 1989, 1967; Seger and Augart, 1994.

claim: Implicit knowledge can be used to guide behaviour despite an inability to verbalise the underlying regularities.
source: The resulting implicit knowledge can be used to guide behaviour despite an inability to verbalise the underlying regularities.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about implicit learning.

claim: Implicit learning of sequences involves medial temporal lobe structures, including the hippocampus, subiculum, and entorhinal cortex.
source: Neurally, implicit learning of sequences involves medial temporal lobe structures, including the hippocampus, subiculum, and entorhinal cortex (Schendan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from Schendan et al., 2003.

claim: The hippocampal–entorhinal system responds to the violation of learnt sequence structures.
source: The hippocampal–entorhinal system also responds to the violation of learnt sequence structures (Kumaran and Maguire, 2006) and signals the likelihood of events in learnt sequences (Strange et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Kumaran and Maguire, 2006.

claim: The hippocampal–entorhinal system signals the likelihood of events in learnt sequences.
source: The hippocampal–entorhinal system also responds to the violation of learnt sequence structures (Kumaran and Maguire, 2006) and signals the likelihood of events in learnt sequences (Strange et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Strange et al., 2005.

claim: Implicit knowledge may be facilitated by an increase in representational similarity as stimuli become embedded into knowledge structures.
source: This may be facilitated by an increase in representational similarity as stimuli become embedded into knowledge structures (Schapiro et al., 2013, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Schapiro et al., 2013, 2012.

claim: The study proposes a specific way in which implicit knowledge may be organised in maps to facilitate goal-directed behaviour.
source: Our results add to this literature by proposing a specific way in which implicit knowledge may be organised in maps to facilitate goal-directed behaviour.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The study did not find clear evidence for the map-like structure outside the hippocampal formation.
source: It is notable that we did not find clear evidence for the map-like structure outside the hippocampal formation, although areas such as the orbitofrontal cortex have been shown to represent cognitive maps of decision spaces (Schuck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a negative finding in the Discussion.

claim: Areas such as the orbitofrontal cortex have been shown to represent cognitive maps of decision spaces.
source: It is notable that we did not find clear evidence for the map-like structure outside the hippocampal formation, although areas such as the orbitofrontal cortex have been shown to represent cognitive maps of decision spaces (Schuck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Schuck et al., 2016.

claim: Neural signals can be recorded in frontal and parietal cortices, reflecting the 'state-prediction errors' that ensue when predicted state relationships are breached during behavioural control.
source: Indeed, we note that neural signals can be recorded in frontal and parietal cortices, reflecting the 'state-prediction errors' that ensue when predicted state relationships are breached during behavioural control (Gläscher et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Gläscher et al., 2010.

claim: Prediction errors in the orbitofrontal cortex during active learning predict later changes in hippocampal representations of the stored model.
source: Similar prediction errors in the orbitofrontal cortex during active learning predict later changes in hippocampal representations of the stored model (Boorman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Boorman et al., 2016.

claim: There is a theoretical account of place and grid activity in the hippocampal formation as state representations in reinforcement learning models.
source: These and similar ideas have led to a theoretical account of place and grid activity in the hippocampal formation as state representations in reinforcement learning models (Stachenfeld et al., 2016, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Stachenfeld et al., 2016, 2014.

claim: The hippocampal formation is important for tasks that rely on associative and relational knowledge.
source: It has long been known that the hippocampal formation is important for tasks that rely on associative and relational knowledge.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The hippocampal formation supports the organisation of stimuli across arbitrary stimulus dimensions such as temporal co-occurrence.
source: It supports the organisation of stimuli across arbitrary stimulus dimensions such as temporal co-occurrence (Schapiro et al., 2013, 2012) or social rank (Kumaran et al., 2012), and organises behaviourally relevant stimulus categories in a hierarchy (McKenzie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Schapiro et al., 2013, 2012.

claim: The hippocampal formation supports the organisation of stimuli across arbitrary stimulus dimensions such as social rank.

claim: Twenty three volunteers aged 18–31 years participated in the fMRI experiment.

source: To avoid local repetitions, we constrained sequences such that at least three objects had to occur between any two presentations of the same object.

claim: Each object was randomly presented in one of two orientations, which were mirror images of each other.
source: Each object was randomly presented in one of two orientations, which were mirror images of each other.

claim: Each experimental block consisted of 133 object presentations.

source: Furthermore, stimulus transitions did not follow the graph structure, but were instead randomised with a constraint that each of the 42 possible object transitions occurred exactly 10 times per block (objects were never repeated).

source: Day 1 of the behavioural experiment was designed to be the same as day 1 of the fMRI experiment, with subjects performing 10 (n = 14) or 12 (n = 12) blocks of the object orientation cover task on object sequences generated according to a random walk along the graph structure.
